newsitem.title: USA: Plan to raise Medicare deductible unlikely to stay.
newsitem.headline: Plan to raise Medicare deductible unlikely to stay.

text.p: A Senate proposal to force affluent senior citizens to pay higher Medicare deductibles may be unworkable and is not likely to raise much money, analysts said Wednesday.

The plan, adopted in the early hours of the morning by the Senate Finance Committee, may cause political and policy headaches while doing little to address the long-term financing problems of Medicare, they said.

"It is unequivocally bad policy. It's inequitable, it's unadministrable and it's likely to be ineffectual," said Robert Reischauer, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution. "It imposes additional costs not on the wealthy, but on the sick wealthy. The healthy wealthy get off scot free."

As part of broad budget legislation, the Senate Finance Committee voted 18-2 for an amendment by Nebraska Democrat Bob Kerrey which for the first time ties deductibles for Medicare Part B doctor's services to income.

The Medicare Part B programme is voluntary, but nearly all eligible seniors choose it as it covers doctor, laboratory, outpatient hospital and other services not provided by the regular Medicare programme.
The current deductible is $100 per year and the monthly premium is $43.80. Once the premium is met, Part B generally covers 80 percent of costs based on Medicare's fee schedule.

Under the new plan, seniors with incomes $50,000 and above and couples with incomes $75,000 and above would face sharply higher out-of-pocket costs. The deductible would rise to $540 a year at the $50,000/$75,000 income level, climbing to $2,160 for individuals making more than $100,000 and couples making more than $125,000.
"I will not back away from the idea that we should not ask lower-income people to subsidise upper-income people who can pay on their own," Kerrey said.

Kerrey said the proposal would penalise people who used more health care services, but said greater utilization did not necessarily equate with health problems. By raising the deductible, seniors might be more efficient health shoppers.
He admitted there were administrative problems, but said they could be worked out.
About 6 percent of Medicare recipients, or 2.4 million people, have income above proposed limits, his office said.

Lawmakers from both parties and President Clinton have suggested the possibility of making affluent seniors pay higher premiums -- not deductibles -- for Part B coverage in an effort to control costs and bring equity to the programme.
They point to long-term forecasts showing a severe financial crisis in the programme without major changes.
Both sides shied away from the issue as too politically charged when working out a balanced budget deal this year.
White House health adviser Chris Jennings said administration officials worried the plan would be complex to administer and opposed adding it to the budget bill.
The proposal is not in the House Medicare bill.
The American Association of Retired Persons, the nation's largest senior citizens group, plans to fight the plan.

Independent analysts questioned how fair the change would be, saying it could have the effect of raising rates for popular Medigap insurance policies that seniors buy to cover deductibles and other services not covered by Medicare.

"Medigap costs would go up. The question is, would they be able to charge people differentials on the basis of income or would they have to raise rates (across the board)?" said Marilyn Moon of the Urban Institute. "If they did, that would be very unfair to low income people."
The Congressional Budget Office in the past has forecast that means-testing Medicare premiums would not generate significant savings, relative to the level needed to balance the budget.
An Urban Institute study looking at the impact of a $1,000 premium for Medicare found payments per person would rise from $100 to $370.
